entry.sum: Vectors are linearly independent when no nontrivial combination of them is $\mathbf 0$, and a basis is an independent list that spans the space, so that every vector has unique coordinates. All bases of a finite-dimensional space have the same length, its dimension: the number of independent parameters needed to describe a vector.
key: c_1\mathbf v_1 + \cdots + c_k\mathbf v_k = \mathbf 0 \implies c_1 = \cdots = c_k = 0
\mathbf u_1, \dots, \mathbf u_k \text{ independent in } \operatorname{span}(\mathbf w_1, \dots, \mathbf w_m) \implies k \le m
\dim F^n = n, \qquad \dim P_n = n + 1, \qquad \dim M_{m \times n} = mn
entry.why: Dimension is the precise form of 'degrees of freedom': it counts the free parameters of a solution set, shows that certain configurations cannot be too large, and gives the degree of a field extension.

links.note: The degree $[L:K]$ of a field extension is the dimension of $L$ as a vector space over $K$, and the tower law $[M:K] = [M:L][L:K]$ comes from multiplying bases.
The linear algebra method bounds the size of a family of sets by showing that associated vectors are independent in a space of known dimension, as in the Oddtown theorem.
A system of $n$ qubits has a state space of dimension $2^n$, with the $2^n$ bit strings as a basis, which is why simulating quantum circuits on classical computers is expensive in general.

blocks.body:
How many numbers does it take to describe a point of a plane through the origin in $\mathbb R^3$? The plane sits in three-dimensional space, but two numbers suffice: choose two non-parallel vectors $\mathbf a, \mathbf b$ in the plane, and every point of the plane is $s\mathbf a + t\mathbf b$ for exactly one pair $(s, t)$. A polynomial of degree at most $3$ needs four numbers, its coefficients, and the solutions of a homogeneous linear system need as many numbers as there are free variables.

This lesson makes 'number of parameters' precise. The crucial fact is that the number does not depend on how the parameters are chosen: any two bases of a space have the same size. That number, the dimension, is the most important invariant of a vector space.

blocks.title: Linear independence
blocks.body:
Vectors $\mathbf v_1, \dots, \mathbf v_k$ in a vector space $V$ ([[vector-spaces]]) are linearly independent if the only way to write $\mathbf 0$ as a combination of them is the trivial way:
$$c_1\mathbf v_1 + \cdots + c_k\mathbf v_k = \mathbf 0 \implies c_1 = \cdots = c_k = 0.$$
Otherwise they are linearly dependent, and an equation $c_1\mathbf v_1 + \cdots + c_k\mathbf v_k = \mathbf 0$ with some $c_i \ne 0$ is a dependence relation.

A list is dependent exactly when one of its vectors is a combination of the others: given a dependence relation with $c_i \ne 0$, divide by $c_i$ and solve for $\mathbf v_i$; conversely, $\mathbf v_i = \sum_{j \ne i} d_j\mathbf v_j$ rearranges to a dependence relation with coefficient $-1$ on $\mathbf v_i$. So independence means that no vector in the list is redundant.

blocks.title: Testing independence
blocks.body:
For vectors in $F^n$, independence is a question about a homogeneous linear system. Put the vectors as the columns of a matrix $A$. Then $c_1\mathbf v_1 + \cdots + c_k\mathbf v_k = A\mathbf c$ ([[matrices]]), so the vectors are independent exactly when $A\mathbf c = \mathbf 0$ has only the solution $\mathbf c = \mathbf 0$. By [[linear-systems]], this happens exactly when the row echelon form of $A$ has a pivot in every column, so that there are no free variables.

Some quick cases:
- A list containing $\mathbf 0$ is dependent, since $1 \cdot \mathbf 0 = \mathbf 0$.
- Two vectors are dependent exactly when one is a multiple of the other.
- In $P_n$ the monomials $1, x, \dots, x^n$ are independent: if $c_0 + c_1x + \cdots + c_nx^n$ is the zero polynomial, all its coefficients are $0$.
- More than $n$ vectors in $F^n$ are always dependent, because a homogeneous system with more unknowns than equations has a nonzero solution. The theorem below extends this to every vector space.

blocks.title: Basis and coordinates
blocks.body:
A basis of $V$ is a list $\mathbf v_1, \dots, \mathbf v_n$ that is linearly independent and spans $V$. Then every $\mathbf v \in V$ can be written as
$$\mathbf v = c_1\mathbf v_1 + \cdots + c_n\mathbf v_n$$
in exactly one way, and $(c_1, \dots, c_n)$ are the coordinates of $\mathbf v$ in this basis.

Spanning gives the existence of the coefficients and independence their uniqueness: if $\sum c_i\mathbf v_i = \sum d_i\mathbf v_i$, then $\sum (c_i - d_i)\mathbf v_i = \mathbf 0$, so $c_i = d_i$ for every $i$. The standard basis of $F^n$ is $\mathbf e_1 = (1, 0, \dots, 0), \dots, \mathbf e_n = (0, \dots, 0, 1)$, and $1, x, \dots, x^n$ is a basis of $P_n$.

blocks.title: Independent lists are no longer than spanning lists
blocks.body: If $\mathbf w_1, \dots, \mathbf w_m$ span $V$ and $\mathbf u_1, \dots, \mathbf u_k \in V$ are linearly independent, then $k \le m$.

Suppose $k > m$; we construct a dependence relation among the $\mathbf u_j$. Since the $\mathbf w_i$ span $V$, each $\mathbf u_j$ is a combination of them:
$$\mathbf u_j = \sum_{i=1}^m a_{ij}\mathbf w_i \qquad (j = 1, \dots, k).$$
Consider the homogeneous system of $m$ equations in the $k$ unknowns $c_1, \dots, c_k$:
$$\sum_{j=1}^k a_{ij}c_j = 0 \qquad (i = 1, \dots, m).$$
Its echelon form has at most $m$ pivots, so with $k > m$ unknowns at least one is free, and setting it to $1$ gives a solution $(c_1, \dots, c_k) \ne \mathbf 0$ ([[linear-systems]]; elimination works over any field). For this solution,
$$\sum_{j=1}^k c_j\mathbf u_j = \sum_{j=1}^k c_j\sum_{i=1}^m a_{ij}\mathbf w_i = \sum_{i=1}^m\Big(\sum_{j=1}^k a_{ij}c_j\Big)\mathbf w_i = \mathbf 0,$$
a nontrivial dependence relation among the $\mathbf u_j$. This contradicts their independence, so $k \le m$.

blocks.title: Shrinking and extending to a basis
blocks.body:
Let $V$ be spanned by a finite list.
1. Every finite spanning list of $V$ contains a basis of $V$. In particular, $V$ has a basis.
2. Every linearly independent list in $V$ can be extended to a basis of $V$.

Key observation: if $\mathbf u_1, \dots, \mathbf u_k$ are independent and $\mathbf v \notin \operatorname{span}(\mathbf u_1, \dots, \mathbf u_k)$, then $\mathbf u_1, \dots, \mathbf u_k, \mathbf v$ are independent. Indeed, in a relation $c_1\mathbf u_1 + \cdots + c_k\mathbf u_k + c\mathbf v = \mathbf 0$, if $c \ne 0$ we could solve for $\mathbf v$ and place it in the span; so $c = 0$, and then all $c_i = 0$ by the independence of the $\mathbf u_i$.

1. Go through a spanning list $\mathbf w_1, \dots, \mathbf w_m$ in order, keeping $\mathbf w_j$ if it is not in the span of the vectors kept so far, and discarding it otherwise. By the observation the kept vectors remain independent. Each discarded vector is a combination of kept ones, so the kept vectors span the same space as all the $\mathbf w_j$, namely $V$. (If $V = \{\mathbf 0\}$, nothing is kept, and the empty list is a basis.)

2. Let $\mathbf w_1, \dots, \mathbf w_m$ span $V$ and let $\mathbf u_1, \dots, \mathbf u_k$ be independent. If the $\mathbf u_i$ do not span $V$, some $\mathbf w_j$ is not in their span (otherwise their span, a subspace containing every $\mathbf w_j$, would be all of $V$); adjoin it. The list stays independent by the observation. Repeat. By the previous theorem an independent list in $V$ has at most $m$ vectors, so the process stops, and it can only stop when the list spans $V$.

blocks.title: Dimension
blocks.body:
A vector space is finite-dimensional if it is spanned by some finite list. By the last theorem it then has a basis. If $\mathbf v_1, \dots, \mathbf v_n$ and $\mathbf v_1', \dots, \mathbf v_{n'}'$ are two bases, the first theorem gives $n \le n'$ (the first list is independent, the second spans) and $n' \le n$, so all bases have the same length. This common length is the dimension $\dim V$. The space $\{\mathbf 0\}$ has the empty list as basis and dimension $0$.

So the dimension is the number of coordinates needed to describe a vector, and it does not depend on the basis.

blocks.title: Counting dimensions
blocks.body:
Let $\dim V = n$. Two consequences make checking a basis much quicker.
- Any $n$ independent vectors form a basis: by part 2 of the theorem on shrinking and extending they extend to a basis, which has exactly $n$ vectors, so nothing was added.
- Any $n$ vectors that span $V$ form a basis: by part 1 of that theorem they contain a basis, which has $n$ vectors, so nothing was removed.

So with the right number of vectors, independence alone or spanning alone suffices. Also, a subspace $U \subseteq V$ is finite-dimensional with $\dim U \le n$, and $\dim U = n$ only when $U = V$. (Build an independent list inside $U$ one vector at a time, adjoining a vector of $U$ outside the current span; it stays independent by the key observation, and has at most $n$ vectors because it is independent in $V$, so the process stops with a basis of $U$. If that basis has $n$ vectors, it is a basis of $V$ by the first point, so $U = V$.) For instance the subspaces of $\mathbb R^2$ have dimension $0$, $1$ or $2$: they are $\{\mathbf 0\}$, the lines through the origin, and $\mathbb R^2$ itself.

The standard spaces:
- $\dim F^n = n$ (standard basis), $\dim P_n = n + 1$ (basis $1, x, \dots, x^n$), and $\dim M_{m \times n} = mn$ (the matrices with one entry $1$ and all others $0$).
- The space $P$ of all polynomials is not finite-dimensional: finitely many polynomials have a largest degree $d$, and $x^{d+1}$ is not in their span.
- The null space of a matrix has dimension equal to the number of free variables. Writing the general solution of $A\mathbf x = \mathbf 0$ as $t_1\mathbf h_1 + \cdots + t_r\mathbf h_r$, one vector $\mathbf h_i$ for each free variable, the $\mathbf h_i$ span the null space by construction, and they are independent because $\mathbf h_i$ has entry $1$ in the position of the $i$-th free variable while every other $\mathbf h_j$ has $0$ there.

blocks.title: A dependent list with no parallel vectors
blocks.body: Are $(1, 2, 3)$, $(4, 5, 6)$, $(7, 8, 9)$ linearly independent? What is the dimension of their span?
blocks.solution:
Row reduce the matrix with these vectors as columns, using $R_2 \to R_2 - 2R_1$, $R_3 \to R_3 - 3R_1$, then $R_3 \to R_3 - 2R_2$:
$$\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 4 & 7 \\ 2 & 5 & 8 \\ 3 & 6 & 9 \end{pmatrix} \to \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 4 & 7 \\ 0 & -3 & -6 \\ 0 & -6 & -12 \end{pmatrix} \to \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 4 & 7 \\ 0 & -3 & -6 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}.$$
The third column has no pivot, so $c_3$ is free and the vectors are dependent. Setting $c_3 = 1$, the second row gives $-3c_2 - 6 = 0$, so $c_2 = -2$, and the first gives $c_1 = -4c_2 - 7 = 1$. Indeed
$$(1, 2, 3) - 2(4, 5, 6) + (7, 8, 9) = (0, 0, 0).$$
The first two vectors are independent (neither is a multiple of the other), and the third lies in their span, so the span is a plane through the origin, of dimension $2$. No two of the three vectors are parallel, yet the three together are dependent: independence is a property of the whole list, not of its pairs.

blocks.title: Coordinates in a different basis
blocks.body: Show that $1, (x - 1), (x - 1)^2$ is a basis of $P_2$, and find the coordinates of $p(x) = x^2 + 3x + 5$ in this basis.
blocks.solution:
Since $\dim P_2 = 3$, three vectors form a basis as soon as they are independent. Suppose $a + b(x - 1) + c(x - 1)^2$ is the zero polynomial. Its coefficient of $x^2$ is $c$, so $c = 0$; then its coefficient of $x$ is $b$, so $b = 0$; then $a = 0$. So the list is independent, hence a basis.

For the coordinates substitute $x = 1 + t$: $p = (1 + t)^2 + 3(1 + t) + 5 = t^2 + 5t + 9$. Hence
$$x^2 + 3x + 5 = 9 + 5(x - 1) + (x - 1)^2,$$
and the coordinates are $(9, 5, 1)$. These are $p(1)$, $p'(1)$ and $p''(1)/2$: coordinates in this basis are exactly the coefficients of the Taylor expansion at $1$ ([[taylor]]).

blocks.title: Oddtown
blocks.body: A town has $n$ residents, who form clubs. Every club has an odd number of members, and every two different clubs have an even number of members in common. Prove that there are at most $n$ clubs.
blocks.solution:
Work in the vector space $\mathbb F_2^n$ over the field $\mathbb F_2 = \{0, 1\}$, with arithmetic modulo $2$. Number the residents $1, \dots, n$, and represent a club $C$ by the vector $\mathbf v_C \in \mathbb F_2^n$ with entry $1$ in position $i$ if resident $i$ belongs to $C$ and $0$ otherwise. For $\mathbf x, \mathbf y \in \mathbb F_2^n$ put $\mathbf x \cdot \mathbf y = x_1y_1 + \cdots + x_ny_n$, computed modulo $2$. Then $\mathbf v_C \cdot \mathbf v_D$ is the number of common members of $C$ and $D$, reduced modulo $2$, and the hypotheses say
$$\mathbf v_C \cdot \mathbf v_C = 1, \qquad \mathbf v_C \cdot \mathbf v_D = 0 \quad (C \ne D).$$
Suppose $\sum_C c_C\mathbf v_C = \mathbf 0$ with coefficients $c_C \in \mathbb F_2$. Take the dot product of both sides with $\mathbf v_D$; by the distributive law modulo $2$ the left side becomes $\sum_C c_C(\mathbf v_C \cdot \mathbf v_D) = c_D$, so $c_D = 0$. This holds for every club $D$, so the club vectors are linearly independent in $\mathbb F_2^n$, which is spanned by the $n$ standard basis vectors. Since independent lists are no longer than spanning lists, there are at most $n$ clubs.

The bound is attained, for example by the $n$ one-member clubs. Working modulo $2$ is the whole trick: it turns 'odd' into $1$ and 'even' into $0$, so the club vectors behave like mutually perpendicular vectors. This is the prototype of the linear algebra method in combinatorics ([[linear-algebra]]).

blocks.body:
- Pairwise independence is not independence (see the first example), and a list containing $\mathbf 0$ or a repeated vector is always dependent.
- A basis must both span and be independent. In an $n$-dimensional space, a list of exactly $n$ vectors needs only one of the two checks; fewer than $n$ vectors never span, and more than $n$ are never independent.
- Dimension depends on the field of scalars: $\mathbb C$ has dimension $1$ over $\mathbb C$ (basis $1$) but dimension $2$ over $\mathbb R$ (basis $1, i$).
- A subspace need not contain any of the standard basis vectors: the line spanned by $(1, 1)$ in $\mathbb R^2$ contains neither $\mathbf e_1$ nor $\mathbf e_2$. A basis of a subspace usually has to be computed, not picked out of a basis of the larger space.
- The solution set of $A\mathbf x = \mathbf b$ with $\mathbf b \ne \mathbf 0$ is not a subspace. Its 'number of parameters' is the dimension of the null space $N(A)$, of which it is a shifted copy.

The rank–nullity theorem of [[linear-maps]] says that, for a linear map, the dimensions of what is lost (the kernel) and of what is reached (the image) add up to the dimension of the domain; this explains the count 'free variables = unknowns minus pivots'. Orthonormal bases are the subject of [[inner-products]], and bases of eigenvectors are the subject of [[eigen]] and [[diagonalization]].

In algebra, the degree of a field extension is a dimension ([[fields-ext]]). A finite field of characteristic $p$ is a vector space over $\mathbb F_p$ of some finite dimension $n$, and choosing a basis shows it has exactly $p^n$ elements ([[finite-fields]]). The Oddtown argument is the model for many dimension arguments in extremal combinatorics ([[set-systems]]).

entry.sum: A linear map $T : V \to W$ between vector spaces respects addition and scalar multiplication; from $F^n$ to $F^m$ these are exactly the maps $\mathbf x \mapsto A\mathbf x$. Its kernel (the vectors sent to $\mathbf 0$) and its image (the vectors reached) are subspaces, and the rank–nullity theorem says that their dimensions add up to $\dim V$.
key: T(a\mathbf u + b\mathbf v) = aT\mathbf u + bT\mathbf v
\dim V = \dim\ker T + \dim\operatorname{im} T
T \text{ injective} \iff \ker T = \{\mathbf 0\}
entry.why: Rank–nullity turns questions of existence and uniqueness into a dimension count: for a square matrix, $A\mathbf x = \mathbf b$ is solvable for every $\mathbf b$ exactly when $A\mathbf x = \mathbf 0$ has only the zero solution.

links.note: A linear differential operator such as $y \mapsto y'' + y$ is a linear map; the general solution of $Ly = f$ is one particular solution plus the kernel of $L$.
Rotations, reflections, projections and shears are linear maps of the plane or space, and composing them corresponds to multiplying their matrices.
A linear error-correcting code is the image of an injective linear map $\mathbb F_2^k \to \mathbb F_2^n$, and also the kernel of a parity-check matrix; rank–nullity relates the two descriptions.

blocks.body:
Rotating the plane, projecting space onto a plane, differentiating a polynomial, evaluating a function at a point: each of these turns sums into sums and multiples into multiples. Such functions are called linear maps, and they are the functions that the structure of a [[vector-spaces|vector space]] is made for.

The central result is a conservation law. A linear map defined on an $n$-dimensional space loses some dimensions (the vectors it sends to $\mathbf 0$) and keeps the rest (the dimension of its image), and the two numbers always add up to $n$. This explains the count 'free variables = unknowns minus pivots' from [[linear-systems]], and it shows, for example, that for square matrices a one-sided inverse is automatically two-sided.

blocks.title: Linear map
blocks.body:
Let $V$ and $W$ be vector spaces over the same field $F$. A function $T : V \to W$ is linear if for all $\mathbf u, \mathbf v \in V$ and $c \in F$
$$T(\mathbf u + \mathbf v) = T\mathbf u + T\mathbf v \qquad \text{and} \qquad T(c\mathbf v) = cT\mathbf v.$$
Equivalently, $T(a\mathbf u + b\mathbf v) = aT\mathbf u + bT\mathbf v$ for all scalars $a, b$. Taking $c = 0$ shows that $T\mathbf 0 = \mathbf 0$.

So a linear map sends every linear combination to the same combination of the images.

blocks.title: Examples, and the matrix of a linear map
blocks.body:
- Every $m \times n$ matrix $A$ gives a linear map $F^n \to F^m$, $\mathbf x \mapsto A\mathbf x$ ([[matrices]]).
- Differentiation $D : P_n \to P_n$, $Dp = p'$, is linear, since $(p + q)' = p' + q'$ and $(cp)' = cp'$. So is $p \mapsto \int_0^x p(t)\,dt$ from $P_n$ to $P_{n+1}$.
- Evaluation $p \mapsto p(2)$ is a linear map $P_n \to \mathbb R$, and $p \mapsto (p(0), p(1), p(2))$ is a linear map $P_n \to \mathbb R^3$.
- Not linear: a translation $\mathbf x \mapsto \mathbf x + \mathbf b$ with $\mathbf b \ne \mathbf 0$ (it moves $\mathbf 0$), and $x \mapsto x^2$ on $\mathbb R$.

A linear map is determined by its values on a basis. If $\mathbf v_1, \dots, \mathbf v_n$ is a basis of $V$ and $\mathbf v = c_1\mathbf v_1 + \cdots + c_n\mathbf v_n$, then $T\mathbf v = c_1T\mathbf v_1 + \cdots + c_nT\mathbf v_n$. Conversely, any vectors $\mathbf w_1, \dots, \mathbf w_n \in W$ are the values of a linear map on the basis, namely $T(\sum c_j\mathbf v_j) = \sum c_j\mathbf w_j$, which is well defined because coordinates are unique ([[basis-dimension]]). For $T : F^n \to F^m$ and the standard basis this says $T\mathbf x = x_1T\mathbf e_1 + \cdots + x_nT\mathbf e_n = A\mathbf x$, where $A$ is the matrix with columns $T\mathbf e_1, \dots, T\mathbf e_n$. So the matrix maps of the first example are all the linear maps $F^n \to F^m$.

The same recipe works in any finite-dimensional spaces once bases are chosen: the matrix of $T$ with respect to bases $\mathbf v_1, \dots, \mathbf v_n$ of $V$ and $\mathbf w_1, \dots, \mathbf w_m$ of $W$ has as its $j$-th column the coordinates of $T\mathbf v_j$. For $D$ on $P_3$ with basis $1, x, x^2, x^3$, the images are $0, 1, 2x, 3x^2$, so
$$[D] = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}.$$
Composing linear maps corresponds to multiplying their matrices, which is the reason for the definition of the matrix product.

blocks.title: Kernel and image
blocks.body:
For a linear map $T : V \to W$, the kernel (or null space) and the image (or range) are
$$\ker T = \{\mathbf v \in V : T\mathbf v = \mathbf 0\}, \qquad \operatorname{im} T = \{T\mathbf v : \mathbf v \in V\}.$$
They are subspaces of $V$ and of $W$: both contain $\mathbf 0 = T\mathbf 0$; if $T\mathbf u = T\mathbf v = \mathbf 0$ then $T(a\mathbf u + b\mathbf v) = \mathbf 0$; and $aT\mathbf u + bT\mathbf v = T(a\mathbf u + b\mathbf v)$ lies in the image. When they are finite-dimensional, $\dim\ker T$ is the nullity and $\dim\operatorname{im} T$ the rank of $T$.

For $T\mathbf x = A\mathbf x$, the kernel is the null space $N(A)$ and the image is the column space of $A$ ([[vector-spaces]]).

blocks.title: Injectivity is read off the kernel
blocks.body: A linear map $T$ is injective if and only if $\ker T = \{\mathbf 0\}$.

If $T$ is injective, then $T\mathbf v = \mathbf 0 = T\mathbf 0$ forces $\mathbf v = \mathbf 0$. Conversely, if $\ker T = \{\mathbf 0\}$ and $T\mathbf u = T\mathbf v$, then $T(\mathbf u - \mathbf v) = \mathbf 0$, so $\mathbf u - \mathbf v \in \ker T$ and $\mathbf u = \mathbf v$.

More generally, $T\mathbf u = T\mathbf v$ exactly when $\mathbf u - \mathbf v \in \ker T$: the kernel measures precisely what information $T$ destroys.

blocks.title: Rank–nullity theorem
blocks.body:
Let $V$ be finite-dimensional and $T : V \to W$ linear. Then $\operatorname{im} T$ is finite-dimensional and
$$\dim V = \dim\ker T + \dim\operatorname{im} T.$$

The kernel is a subspace of the finite-dimensional space $V$, so it has a basis $\mathbf u_1, \dots, \mathbf u_k$ ([[basis-dimension]]). Extend it to a basis $\mathbf u_1, \dots, \mathbf u_k, \mathbf v_1, \dots, \mathbf v_r$ of $V$, so that $\dim V = k + r$. We show that $T\mathbf v_1, \dots, T\mathbf v_r$ is a basis of $\operatorname{im} T$; then $\dim\operatorname{im} T = r$ and we are done.

Spanning. A vector of the image has the form $T\mathbf v$ with $\mathbf v = \sum a_i\mathbf u_i + \sum b_j\mathbf v_j$, and then $T\mathbf v = \sum a_iT\mathbf u_i + \sum b_jT\mathbf v_j = \sum b_jT\mathbf v_j$, because each $T\mathbf u_i = \mathbf 0$.

Independence. If $\sum b_jT\mathbf v_j = \mathbf 0$, then $T(\sum b_j\mathbf v_j) = \mathbf 0$, so $\sum b_j\mathbf v_j$ lies in $\ker T$ and equals $\sum a_i\mathbf u_i$ for some scalars $a_i$. Then $\sum a_i\mathbf u_i - \sum b_j\mathbf v_j = \mathbf 0$ is a relation among the vectors of a basis of $V$, so all $a_i$ and all $b_j$ are $0$.

blocks.title: What rank–nullity says
blocks.body:
For an $m \times n$ matrix $A$ whose echelon form has $p$ pivots, the null space has dimension $n - p$, one for each free variable ([[basis-dimension]]). Rank–nullity then says that the column space has dimension $p$. So the rank of a matrix is its number of pivots; in fact the pivot columns of $A$ itself form a basis of its column space, as the first example below illustrates.

The theorem gives several conclusions for free.
- If $\dim V > \dim W$, then $T : V \to W$ cannot be injective, since $$\dim\ker T = \dim V - \dim\operatorname{im} T \ge \dim V - \dim W > 0$$. This is again 'more unknowns than equations gives a nonzero solution'.
- If $\dim V < \dim W$, then $T$ cannot be surjective, since $\dim\operatorname{im} T \le \dim V < \dim W$.
- If $\dim V = \dim W$ is finite, then: $T$ injective $\iff$ $\ker T = \{\mathbf 0\}$ $\iff$ $\dim\operatorname{im} T = \dim W$ $\iff$ $T$ surjective. (The last step uses that a subspace of $W$ of full dimension is $W$.) For a square matrix this says: $A\mathbf x = \mathbf b$ is solvable for every $\mathbf b$ if and only if $A\mathbf x = \mathbf 0$ has only the solution $\mathbf 0$, and in that case every solution is unique and $A$ is invertible.

A consequence promised in [[matrices]]: if $A$ and $B$ are $n \times n$ matrices with $AB = I$, then $BA = I$. Indeed, $B\mathbf x = \mathbf 0$ implies $\mathbf x = AB\mathbf x = \mathbf 0$, so $\mathbf x \mapsto B\mathbf x$ is injective, hence bijective by the last point. Its inverse map $S$ is linear (if $S\mathbf y_1 = \mathbf x_1$ and $S\mathbf y_2 = \mathbf x_2$, then $B(a\mathbf x_1 + b\mathbf x_2) = a\mathbf y_1 + b\mathbf y_2$, so $S(a\mathbf y_1 + b\mathbf y_2) = a\mathbf x_1 + b\mathbf x_2$), so it is given by a matrix $C$, and $BC = CB = I$. Then $A = A(BC) = (AB)C = C$, and therefore $BA = BC = I$.

blocks.title: Kernel and image of a matrix
blocks.body:
Find bases of the kernel and the image of $T : \mathbb R^4 \to \mathbb R^3$, $T\mathbf x = A\mathbf x$, where
$$A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 0 & 1 \\ 2 & 4 & 1 & 4 \\ 3 & 6 & 1 & 5 \end{pmatrix}.$$
blocks.solution:
Row reduce with $R_2 \to R_2 - 2R_1$, $R_3 \to R_3 - 3R_1$, then $R_3 \to R_3 - R_2$:
$$\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 0 & 1 \\ 2 & 4 & 1 & 4 \\ 3 & 6 & 1 & 5 \end{pmatrix} \to \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix} \to \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}.$$
The pivots are in columns $1$ and $3$, so $x_2 = s$ and $x_4 = t$ are free. The equations $x_3 + 2x_4 = 0$ and $x_1 + 2x_2 + x_4 = 0$ give $x_3 = -2t$ and $x_1 = -2s - t$, so
$$\ker T = \{s(-2, 1, 0, 0) + t(-1, 0, -2, 1) : s, t \in \mathbb R\},$$
with basis $(-2, 1, 0, 0)$, $(-1, 0, -2, 1)$: the nullity is $2$.

The image is spanned by the four columns of $A$. The pivot columns, $(1, 2, 3)$ and $(0, 1, 1)$, are independent (not multiples of each other), and the other two are combinations of them: column $2$ is twice column $1$, and column $4$ is $(1, 4, 5) = (1, 2, 3) + 2(0, 1, 1)$. So $(1, 2, 3)$, $(0, 1, 1)$ is a basis of the image, the rank is $2$, and indeed $2 + 2 = 4 = \dim\mathbb R^4$.

The image is a plane in $\mathbb R^3$. Both basis vectors satisfy $b_3 = b_1 + b_2$, and that equation defines a plane, so $\operatorname{im} T = \{(b_1, b_2, b_3) : b_3 = b_1 + b_2\}$: the system $A\mathbf x = \mathbf b$ is solvable exactly when $b_3 = b_1 + b_2$.

blocks.title: Differentiation and the equation p − p′ = q
blocks.body:
1. Find the kernel and image of $D : P_3 \to P_3$, $Dp = p'$, and check rank–nullity.
2. Show that for every polynomial $q$ of degree at most $n$ there is exactly one polynomial $p$ of degree at most $n$ with $p - p' = q$, and find it for $q = x^3$.
blocks.solution:
1. $p' = 0$ exactly when $p$ is constant, so $\ker D$ is the space of constants, of dimension $1$. The image consists of the derivatives of polynomials of degree at most $3$, which are exactly the polynomials of degree at most $2$ (each $a + bx + cx^2$ is the derivative of $ax + \frac b2x^2 + \frac c3x^3$), so $\operatorname{im} D = P_2$, of dimension $3$. And $1 + 3 = 4 = \dim P_3$. As a map from $P_3$ to itself, $D$ is neither injective nor surjective, as rank–nullity requires once the kernel is nonzero.

2. Let $T : P_n \to P_n$, $Tp = p - p'$; it is linear. If $p \ne 0$ has degree $d$, then $p'$ is $0$ or has degree less than $d$, so $p' \ne p$ and $Tp \ne 0$. Thus $\ker T = \{0\}$, and since $T$ maps $P_n$ to itself, rank–nullity makes $T$ surjective as well. So $p - p' = q$ has exactly one solution in $P_n$ for every $q \in P_n$.

To find it, note that $D^{n+1} = 0$ on $P_n$, so
$$(I - D)(I + D + D^2 + \cdots + D^n) = I - D^{n+1} = I,$$
and $p = q + q' + q'' + \cdots + q^{(n)}$. For $q = x^3$ this gives $p = x^3 + 3x^2 + 6x + 6$. Check: $p' = 3x^2 + 6x + 6$, so $p - p' = x^3$.

Notice the logic: existence was deduced from uniqueness, without any construction; the explicit formula was a bonus.

blocks.title: Polynomial interpolation without formulas
blocks.body: Let $x_0, \dots, x_n$ be distinct real numbers. Show that for any $y_0, \dots, y_n$ there is exactly one polynomial $p$ of degree at most $n$ with $p(x_i) = y_i$ for all $i$. Then find $p(4)$ if $p$ has degree at most $3$ and $p(0) = 1$, $p(1) = 2$, $p(2) = 4$, $p(3) = 8$.
blocks.solution:
Consider the evaluation map $E : P_n \to \mathbb R^{n+1}$, $E(p) = (p(x_0), \dots, p(x_n))$, which is linear. Its kernel consists of the polynomials of degree at most $n$ that vanish at $n + 1$ distinct points. A nonzero polynomial of degree at most $n$ has at most $n$ roots ([[polynomials-roots]]), so $\ker E = \{0\}$ and $E$ is injective. Both spaces have dimension $n + 1$, so $E$ is also surjective. Surjectivity says that every list $(y_0, \dots, y_n)$ is attained, and injectivity that it is attained only once.

For the numbers, use the polynomials
$$\binom x0 = 1, \quad \binom x1 = x, \quad \binom x2 = \frac{x(x-1)}{2}, \quad \binom x3 = \frac{x(x-1)(x-2)}{6}.$$
They have degrees $0, 1, 2, 3$, so they are independent (compare leading coefficients, as in [[basis-dimension]]) and form a basis of $P_3$. At a non-negative integer $k$ they take the values $\binom kj$ of binomial coefficients, which are $0$ for $j > k$. Hence for $k = 0, 1, 2, 3$,
$$\binom k0 + \binom k1 + \binom k2 + \binom k3 = \sum_{j=0}^k \binom kj = 2^k.$$
So $p(x) = \binom x0 + \binom x1 + \binom x2 + \binom x3$ satisfies all four conditions, and by uniqueness it is the polynomial in question. Therefore
$$p(4) = 1 + 4 + 6 + 4 = 15,$$
not $16$: a cubic that agrees with $2^x$ at four points need not agree at a fifth.

blocks.body:
- $\mathbf x \mapsto A\mathbf x + \mathbf b$ is not linear unless $\mathbf b = \mathbf 0$ (such maps are called affine). A quick first test: if $T\mathbf 0 \ne \mathbf 0$, then $T$ is not linear. Passing the test proves nothing, though; $x \mapsto x^2$ passes it.
- Rank–nullity involves the dimension of the domain, not of the codomain.
- 'Injective if and only if surjective' needs $\dim V = \dim W < \infty$. On the infinite-dimensional space $P$ of all polynomials, $D$ is surjective but not injective, and $p \mapsto xp$ is injective but not surjective.
- The column space of $A$ is spanned by the pivot columns of $A$ itself, not of its echelon form. Row operations preserve the null space but change the column space: in the first example, every column of the echelon form has third entry $0$, while $(1, 2, 3)$ does not.
- The matrix of a linear map depends on the chosen bases; the map itself does not.

A square matrix is invertible exactly when its kernel is $\{\mathbf 0\}$, and [[determinants]] test this with a single number. The kernel of $T - \lambda I$ is the eigenspace for $\lambda$ ([[eigen]]), and choosing bases in which the matrix of a map becomes simple is the theme of [[diagonalization]], [[jordan]] and the [[svd]]. Rank–nullity is the linear-algebra case of the first isomorphism theorem, which for groups and rings says that the image is isomorphic to the quotient by the kernel ([[group-homomorphisms]], [[rings]]).

For a linear differential equation $Ly = f$, the solutions are one particular solution plus $\ker L$, and for an equation of order $n$ with constant coefficients $\dim\ker L = n$ ([[ode-linear]]). Linear maps between spaces with inner products have adjoints, which leads to the [[spectral-theorem]].
